scenario: new small-joint synovitis in a middle-aged woman
text: The patient, a 44-year-old woman, presented with a six-week history of pain and swelling across the knuckles and finger joints of both hands, with morning stiffness lasting over an hour; the plan is to refer to rheumatology.
rationale: suspected persistent synovitis of the small joints: urgent referral; rheumatoid factor test when synovitis is found

scenario: referral held back for blood results
text: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies have been requested, and the rheumatology referral will be sent once the results are back.
rationale: urgent referral does not wait for antibodies or inflammatory markers

scenario: established disease, flare in wrists and knees
text: He has established rheumatoid arthritis and presented with a flare of pain and swelling in both wrists and knees; the plan is a short course of oral steroids.
rationale: short-term glucocorticoids for a flare in established disease

scenario: classic first MTP presentation, NSAID with cover
text: The patient, a 52-year-old man, woke with a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender big toe joint; the working diagnosis is a gout flare, and the plan is an anti-inflammatory with omeprazole cover.
rationale: suspect gout from overnight severe pain, redness and swelling at the first MTP; first-line flare treatment; PPI cover with an NSAID

scenario: third flare in a year, allopurinol after the flare
text: This is his third gout flare in twelve months, and the plan is to discuss starting allopurinol once the flare has settled.
rationale: multiple flares: offer urate-lowering therapy, begun a few weeks after the flare settles, allopurinol or febuxostat first line

scenario: urate measured during a flare taken as excluding gout
text: Serum urate measured during the flare was 320 micromol per litre, which was taken as ruling out gout.
rationale: a urate below 360 during a flare does not exclude gout; recheck once the flare has settled

scenario: typical history, X-ray requested to confirm
text: The patient, a 61-year-old woman, presented with a year of knee pain on walking and stairs with a few minutes of stiffness in the morning; the plan is an X-ray of both knees to confirm osteoarthritis.
rationale: osteoarthritis is diagnosed clinically at 45 or over with activity-related pain and brief morning stiffness; imaging is not routine

scenario: glucosamine and paracetamol advised
text: She was advised that a course of glucosamine and regular paracetamol should help her knee osteoarthritis.
rationale: paracetamol is not offered routinely and glucosamine is not offered for osteoarthritis

scenario: young man, inflammatory back pain, family history
text: The patient, a 29-year-old man, presented with a year of pain in his lower back that wakes him in the early hours and eases once he gets moving; his brother has ankylosing spondylitis.
rationale: back pain starting before 45 and lasting over 3 months with the referral criteria: night waking, easing with movement, a close relative with the disease

scenario: psoriasis with new joint and heel symptoms
text: He has plaque psoriasis and reported new pain and swelling in several finger joints with a swollen, tender right heel.
rationale: psoriatic arthritis suspected in a person with psoriasis: refer to rheumatology

scenario: older woman starting long-term prednisolone
text: The patient, a 68-year-old woman, is starting long-term prednisolone for a rheumatological condition; the plan is to reassess in six months.
rationale: fracture risk assessment for people over 50 starting oral steroids

scenario: mechanical back pain without red flags, MRI requested
text: The patient, a 38-year-old man, presented with four weeks of mechanical low back pain without leg symptoms or red flags; the plan is to request a lumbar spine MRI to see what is going on.
rationale: imaging is not routine for low back pain outside specialist care

scenario: paracetamol and codeine before an NSAID
text: The plan for his acute non-specific low back pain is regular paracetamol with codeine; he has not tried an anti-inflammatory.
rationale: weak opioids are reserved for when an NSAID cannot be used or has failed; opioids are not routine for acute low back pain

scenario: fibromyalgia, gabapentinoid started
text: The working diagnosis is fibromyalgia, and the plan is to start pregabalin for her widespread pain.
rationale: gabapentinoids are not started for chronic primary pain

scenario: new temporal headache with jaw claudication
text: The patient, a 74-year-old woman, presented with a new headache over the right temple, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and aching in the jaw when chewing.
rationale: headache with features suggesting giant cell arteritis: evaluate for investigation or referral

scenario: single raised clinic reading, treatment started
text: Clinic blood pressure was 152 over 94 on repeat measurement today, and the plan is to start amlodipine.
rationale: a clinic reading between 140/90 and 180/120 needs ambulatory monitoring to confirm the diagnosis before treatment

scenario: new diagnosis, metformin alone
text: The working diagnosis is newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c of 58, and the plan is to start metformin alongside dietary advice.
rationale: first-line treatment without comorbidity is modified-release metformin with an SGLT-2 inhibitor

scenario: new episode, antidepressant first
text: The working diagnosis is mild depression, a first episode, and the plan is to start sertraline.
rationale: antidepressants are not routinely first line for less severe depression; discuss the treatment options

scenario: dysphagia in a man in his fifties
text: The patient, a 58-year-old man, presented with four weeks of indigestion and difficulty swallowing solid food.
rationale: dysphagia: two-week cancer referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer

scenario: young woman, coeliac screen planned
text: The patient, a 26-year-old woman with bloating and an alternating bowel habit, has a working diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome; the plan is a coeliac screen and routine bloods.
rationale: tests to exclude other diagnoses in people meeting IBS criteria include coeliac serology; offer serological testing in IBS

scenario: positive serology, gluten-free diet started early
text: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies were positive, and the patient has been advised to cut gluten out of her diet straight away.
rationale: positive serology: refer for biopsy; gluten stays in the diet until a specialist confirms the diagnosis

scenario: urinary infection with new confusion and abnormal vital signs
text: The patient, a 71-year-old woman with a urinary infection, presented with a temperature of 39.2, a heart rate of 118, a respiratory rate of 24 and new confusion.
rationale: possible infection: think sepsis; new altered mental state is a high-risk criterion, refer for emergency care

scenario: antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, causative antibiotic continued
text: She developed profuse diarrhoea a week into a course of co-amoxiclav for a chest infection, and stool testing confirmed Clostridioides difficile; the plan is to finish the co-amoxiclav and start treatment.
rationale: review and stop the existing antibiotic unless essential; antibiotic choice follows table 1

scenario: man with fever and perineal pain
text: The patient, a 47-year-old man, presented with fever, perineal pain and pain on passing urine; the working diagnosis is acute prostatitis, and the plan is a two-week course of an antibiotic.
rationale: offer an antibiotic; midstream urine for culture before it is taken

scenario: loin pain and fever, nitrofurantoin chosen
text: The working diagnosis is acute pyelonephritis in a 34-year-old woman with loin pain and fever, and the plan is a three-day course of nitrofurantoin.
rationale: antibiotic choice and course follow table 1, which does not include nitrofurantoin; midstream urine before antibiotics

scenario: older man, confused, tachypnoeic
text: The working diagnosis is community-acquired pneumonia in a 79-year-old man who is newly confused with a respiratory rate of 32.
rationale: CRB65 scoring; confusion, respiratory rate and age score 3, hospital referral considered at 2 or more

scenario: pulsatile mass with abdominal pain
text: Examination revealed a pulsatile, expansile mass in the abdomen of a 72-year-old man presenting with abdominal pain.
rationale: symptomatic AAA considered: immediate bedside ultrasound and vascular discussion; think about rupture with new abdominal pain

scenario: change in bowel habit and weight loss
text: The patient, a 62-year-old man, presented with six weeks of looser stools and has lost weight without trying; the plan is a stool test for blood and routine bloods.
rationale: quantitative FIT to guide referral when bowel habit changes or weight is lost with abdominal symptoms

scenario: student with fever and non-blanching rash
text: The patient, a 19-year-old student, presented with fever, headache, neck stiffness and a spreading rash that does not fade under a glass; the plan is immediate transfer to hospital and an antibiotic injection before the ambulance arrives.
rationale: non-blanching rash: strongly suspect meningococcal disease; ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin outside hospital unless it delays transfer

condition: urinary tract infection in a child
scenario: 4-year-old, positive dipstick
text: The patient, a 4-year-old girl, presented with two days of fever and offensive-smelling urine; dipstick was positive for leucocytes and nitrites, and the plan is antibiotics.
rationale: children 3 and over: urine-testing strategy in table 2; antibiotics for lower UTI in a child over 3 months

scenario: 18-month-old, fever without source
text: An 18-month-old boy has had a temperature of 39 for two days with no obvious source; he is drinking well and has no rash.
rationale: feverish child: traffic-light assessment of how ill the child is

scenario: 3-year-old with clinical dehydration
text: A 3-year-old with two days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea has dry lips and has passed little urine but is alert and tolerating small sips; the plan is oral rehydration solution.
rationale: clinical dehydration in a child: rehydrate with low-osmolarity ORS

scenario: negated findings
text: He denied joint pain, swelling or morning stiffness, and there is no family history of inflammatory arthritis.
rationale: negated findings and absent family history

scenario: family history only
text: Her mother had rheumatoid arthritis and her father had gout.
rationale: family history, not the patient's condition

scenario: negated associated conditions
text: He has no history of psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or uveitis.
rationale: negated findings

scenario: past history without a current condition
text: Past medical history: appendicectomy at age 12; no regular medication.
rationale: past history with no condition in the corpus

condition: recurrent gout with CKD on a diuretic
scenario: second flare this year, colchicine, ULT deferred, diuretic review
text: The patient, a 66-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 3 who takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension, presented with a second flare of gout in the right knee this year. Examination showed a warm, swollen right knee with reduced range of movement. He is otherwise well with no fever. The working diagnosis is a gout flare on a background of recurrent gout. The plan is to treat the flare with colchicine, to discuss starting urate-lowering therapy once it has settled, and to review his diuretic.
rationale: first-line flare treatment; offer urate-lowering therapy for multiple flares, CKD stage 3 to 5 and diuretic therapy; begin it a few weeks after the flare settles

scenario: eight weeks of hand synovitis, urgent referral without waiting for bloods
text: The patient, a 51-year-old woman, presented with eight weeks of pain and swelling in her wrists and the knuckles of both hands, worst in the morning with stiffness lasting about two hours. She has struggled to open jars and has been dropping things. She has no psoriasis, no recent infection and no back pain. Examination showed synovitis at three knuckle joints and both wrists. The working diagnosis is early inflammatory arthritis. The plan is to check inflammatory markers, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, and to refer to rheumatology urgently without waiting for the results.
rationale: urgent referral for small-joint synovitis regardless of blood results; rheumatoid factor when synovitis is found

scenario: overweight woman, clinical diagnosis, exercise, weight, topical NSAID
text: The patient, a 58-year-old woman with a BMI of 33, presented with two years of right knee pain that is worse on stairs and after walking, with a few minutes of stiffness in the morning. There is no locking, giving way or night pain. Examination showed bony enlargement and crepitus without an effusion. The working diagnosis is knee osteoarthritis. The plan is a referral to physiotherapy for a strengthening programme, support with weight loss, and a topical anti-inflammatory gel to use as needed.
rationale: clinical diagnosis; therapeutic exercise; weight loss support; topical NSAID for knee osteoarthritis

scenario: raised clinic readings, ABPM, organ damage tests, risk assessment
text: The patient, a 55-year-old man, attended for a blood pressure check after a pharmacy reading of 160 over 100. Clinic blood pressure today was 158 over 96 on repeat. He has no symptoms and does not smoke; his father had a stroke at 60. The working diagnosis is suspected hypertension. The plan is a 24-hour blood pressure monitor to check whether the pressure is genuinely raised, with blood tests, a urine sample and an ECG to look for organ damage, and a QRISK calculation.
rationale: ambulatory monitoring to confirm; tests for organ damage and cardiovascular risk while waiting; the tests to offer

scenario: older woman with confusion, tachypnoea and hypotension, admitted
text: The patient, a 74-year-old woman, presented with three days of productive cough, fever and right-sided chest pain on breathing in. Her daughter reports she is mildly confused; her respiratory rate is 28 and blood pressure 96 over 58. She has COPD and lives alone. The working diagnosis is community-acquired pneumonia. The plan is to admit to hospital for assessment.
rationale: CRB65 scoring; confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age all score, hospital referral at 2 or more

condition: first episode of less severe depression
scenario: three months of low mood, PHQ-9 14, SSRI planned
text: The patient, a 34-year-old man, presented with three months of low mood, poor sleep, reduced appetite and loss of interest in his usual activities, with difficulty concentrating at work. He denied thoughts of self-harm and has good support from his partner. PHQ-9 score was 14. The working diagnosis is a first episode of mild depression. The plan is to start an SSRI and review in four weeks.
rationale: antidepressants are not routinely first line for less severe depression; discuss the options
